 DELAWARE BASIN MIDSTREAM LLC’S REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL
                        FOR DECISION

         Delaware Basin Midstream LLC (“DBM”) files this Reply to Exceptions to the Proposal
for Decision (the “PFD”).1 The deadline to file this Reply is September 9, 2026. Therefore, this
Reply is timely filed.2 In support, DBM respectfully shows as follows:
                                                I.       SUMMARY
         Various intervenors ask the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) to adopt
the PFD and deny the Applications in Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475 (the “Applications”), urging
that the need for Import Path 2 has not been shown.3 The Commission, however, should reject the
PFD’s finding that the need for the proposed transmission lines has not been established.4 First,
contrary to the PFD’s conclusion, the Commission adopted the Permian Basin Reliability Plan
(“PBRP”) through a deliberate, expert-driven, and legislatively-directed process. Second, the
PFD’s approach would create an untenable and endless loop by requiring ERCOT to re-justify the
entire PBRP every time ERCOT refined a forecast even though ERCOT never withdrew the PBRP.
For these reasons, DBM asks the Commission to (a) reject the PFD’s need findings; and (b) find
that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public
under Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.056(a).
                                II.   DISCUSSION
    A. Commission Counsel’s recent memorandum in Docket No. 59336 confirms the
         deliberate process through which the Commission adopted the PBRP.
         Echoing the PFD, some intervenors complain that the PBRP solely relied on the S&P
Global Study.5 However, Commission Counsel’s recent memorandum in Docket No. 59336,
addressing PBRP Import Path 3, laid out the expert-driven process by which the PBRP was

 adopted. Specifically, Commission Counsel proposed adoption of the following findings of fact in
Docket No. 59336:

                 70F. ERCOT evaluated several transmission-level alternatives to the proposed
                 transmission facilities and found that none of them more efficiently resolve all the
                 reliability issues identified by ERCOT’s analysis.

                 70G. The Commission and ERCOT evaluated three alternative import paths
                 options—a 345-kV, a 500-kV, and a 765-kV option. The Commission approved the
                 765-kV option, which includes these proposed transmission facilities. The
                 Commission’s evaluation incorporated information received through public
                 workshops, ERCOT working group meetings, formal requests for information, and
                 other input from various stakeholders and industry experts regarding the carrying
                 capacity, estimated costs, engineering, procurement, and construction of the 765-
                 kV alternative relative to the 345-kV and 500-kV options presented by ERCOT in
                 the [PBRP]. Based on the information considered and evaluated, the Commission
                 approved the 765-kV option and ordered the applicable transmission service
                 providers to file CCN applications for the identified 765-kV import projects. Under
                 the Commission’s order, the applicants are responsible for constructing, operating,
                 and maintaining the upgrades included in the applicant’s application; therefore, the
                 applicants did not independently evaluate alternatives.

                 70H. . . . The projects recommended in the [PBRP] were the result of months of
                 engagement between ERCOT, the Commission, transmission service providers,
                 and other stakeholders. Through this process, ERCOT evaluated alternatives and
                 identified the specific set of transmission system improvements that are needed to
                 reliably serve the Permian Basin region. The Commission approved [PBRP] and
                 exempted the approved projects from the further Regional Planning Group review.

                 70I. Distribution alternatives to the proposed transmission facilities would not
                 resolve the identified reliability issues on the transmission system.

                 70J. Adding transformers, upgrading voltages, or bundling conductors for
                 existing facilities would also fail to satisfy the need for the proposed transmission
                 facilities.6




        6
           See Joint Application of AEP Texas Inc. and City of San Antonio, Acting by and through the City Public
Service Board (CPS Energy) to Amend Their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Howard to Solstice
765-kV Single-Circuit Transmission Line in Atascosa, Bandera, Bexar, Crocket, Edwards, Kerr, Kinney, Medina,
Pecos, Real, Sutton, Terrell, Uvalde, and Val Verde Counties, Docket No. 59336, Commission Counsel Memorandum,
at 5–7 (Sept. 3, 2026).


DBM’s Reply Exceptions to PFD                                                                         Page 3 of 7
        That is the antithesis of the simplistic and thoughtless adoption of the PBRP implied by the
PFD and other intervenors. It also severely undercuts the PFD’s suggestion that the PBRP suffered
from a “lack of robust stakeholder input.”7
       This deliberative process is the exact reason why ERCOT’s recommendation of the PBRP
is entitled to great weight under Rule 25.101.8 The PFD ignores the PBRP adoption process and
refuses to give great weight to ERCOT’s recommendation of the PBRP because, in part, ERCOT
purportedly made no separate “credibility finding” on the S&P Global Study load forecasts.9 But
nothing in Rule 25.101 requires ERCOT to issue an explicit credibility finding on individual
underlying studies as a prerequisite to its recommendation receiving great weight. The provision
requires only that ERCOT recommend the project as a reliability measure; the PFD ignores the
fact that ERCOT found the S&P Global Study credible through its recommendation of the PBRP.
And, importantly, the Commission itself adopted the PBRP, after its own robust consideration
process. For these very reasons, Commission Counsel recommended the adoption of the following
ordering paragraphs in Docket No. 59336:

                  70A. The [PBRP] defined three 765-kV import paths that are needed to reliably
                  serve the Permian Basin.

                  ...

                  70B. The [PBRP] establishes a need for additional service in the Permian Basin
                  region to serve existing and projected electrical loads

                  ...

                  70E. The applicants demonstrated a reasonable need for the proposed
                  transmission facilities.10

       The PFD disregards the time and effort expended by ERCOT and the Commission in
adopting the PBRP—public workshops, working-group meetings, formal requests for information,
and stakeholder and industry-expert input—and instead found that the Applicants did not satisfy

            See PFD at 92.
       8

       9

       10

DBM’s Reply Exceptions to PFD                                                            Page 4 of 7
 the need requirement. Conversely, the orders in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 determined that the
PBRP established the need for additional service in the Permian Basin region, and that Import Path
1 was part of the solution to meet that need.11 The PFD in Docket No. 59336 reached the same
conclusion in Import Path 3.12
        As Commission Staff points out, the PFD’s analysis of need disregards the only logical
conclusion from the Commission’s findings of need in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 (which
together comprise Import Path 1). The only logical conclusion is that the “PBRP itself establishes
the need for the Permian Basin Region as a whole,” and all three import paths (including Import
Path 2 at issue in the PFD) within the PBRP are part of the solution to meet that need.13 The
Commission should reject the PFD’s finding on need and, thereby, rule consistently with both (a)
its findings in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315, and (b) Commission Counsel’s memorandum in
Docket No. 59336.
    B. The PFD’s approach creates an endless loop of re-forecasting for adoption of a
        reliability project.
        The PFD suggests that ERCOT’s recommendation to adopt the PBRP is not entitled to
great weight because ERCOT lowered certain load projections after adoption of the PBRP.14 That
reasoning is unworkable when taken to its logical end. Load forecasting is a continuous effort. If
a downward revision obligated ERCOT to re-run and re-justify the entire PBRP, then ERCOT’s
next forecast refinement would compel yet another PBRP reassessment, and another reassessment
after that—an infinite, endless loop in which no reliability plan could ever be adjudicated against
a stable record, and no CCN application built on a Commission-approved plan could ever be
decided. Nothing in PURA or the Commission’s rules requires a utility to chase a perpetually
moving forecast in order to vindicate a reliability plan that the Commission has already approved.

Necessity for the Longshore Switch-Drill Hole Switch 765-kV Transmission Line Project in Andrews, Culberson,
Ector, Glasscock, Howard, Loving, Martin, Midland, Reeves, and Winkler Counties, Docket No. 59029, Order, at 16
(Finding of Fact No. 113) (Aug. 28, 2026); See Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC to Amend its
Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the Dinosaur Switch-Longshore Switch 765-kV Transmission Line
Project in Borden, Bosque, Brown, Callahan, Coke, Coleman, Comanche, Eastland, Erath, Glasscock, Hamilton,
Hood, Howard, Jones, Mitchell, Nolan, Runnels, Shackelford, Somervell, Stephens, Sterling, and Taylor Counties,
Docket No. 59315, Order, at 27 (Finding of Fact No. 59A) (Aug. 28, 2026);
        12
             See Docket No. 59336, SOAH Proposal for Decision with Memorandum, at 39 (July 27, 2026).
        13
             See Commission Staff’s Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision, at 9 (Sept. 2, 2026).
        14
             PFD at 90–92, 181 (Proposed Findings of Fact Nos. 132–140).


DBM’s Reply Exceptions to PFD                                                                        Page 5 of 7
        Neither the Commission nor ERCOT withdrew or amended the PBRP. As the Applicants
explain, the later forecasting methodology “did not withdraw, amend, or supersede the PBRP[;]”
the 2025 Regional Transmission Plan applied the updated methodology and “still included the
765[-]kV import paths in its base assumptions,” and ERCOT “still found all three 765 kV import
paths to be necessary and essential.”15 Staff confirms that ERCOT “has not deviated from or re-
evaluated its determination that the PBRP 765-kV import paths remain necessary since initially
recommending those import paths.”16 Requiring an applicant to revisit ERCOT’s recommendation
and the Commission’s adoption of a reliability plan would effectively substitute an ALJ’s analysis
for ERCOT and the Commission in the reliability plan adoption process. As DBM has explained,
if the PBRP is to be reconsidered in light of changed circumstances, that is a decision for the
Commission—which has not rescinded the PBRP—not for the ALJs.17




       15
            Docket No. 59475, Applicants’ Exceptions to the PFD, at 8, 34 (Sept. 2, 2026).
       16
            Staff Exceptions at 12.
       17
            See Delaware Basin Midstream LLC’s Exceptions to PFD at 8–9 (Sept. 2, 2026); PURA § 39.151.


DBM’s Reply Exceptions to PFD                                                                     Page 6 of 7
                                 III.   CONCLUSION AND PRAYER
       For these reasons, DBM prays that the Commission (1) reject the PFD’s findings and
conclusions on need, including Proposed Conclusion of Law Nos. 13–14; (2) find that Import Path
2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public under PURA
§ 37.056(a); and (3) grant DBM such other and further relief to which it may be entitled.


                                             Respectfully submitted,
